what_its_for: Bevacizumab-bvzr is a cancer medicine used to treat several types of cancer, including certain cancers of the colon, rectum, lung, kidney, brain, cervix, and ovary. It works by blocking a protein in your body that helps tumors grow new blood vessels. Without new blood vessels, the tumor has a harder time growing and spreading.
how_to_take: This medicine is given by a nurse or doctor as an intravenous (IV) infusion directly into your vein. You will receive it at a clinic or hospital. Your first infusion will take about 90 minutes. If you tolerate it well, later infusions may be shorter, around 60 minutes and then 30 minutes. You should not try to give this medicine to yourself at home.
dosing: Your doctor will decide the right dose for you based on your body weight, the type of cancer being treated, and the other medicines you are taking. Doses are typically given every 2 or 3 weeks, often alongside chemotherapy. Always follow your doctor's specific instructions — never change your dosing schedule without talking to your doctor first.
missed_dose: Because this medicine is given by healthcare professionals in a clinic or hospital, it is important to keep all of your scheduled appointments. If you miss or need to reschedule an appointment, call your doctor or clinic right away so they can set up a new time for you. Do not skip doses without talking to your doctor.
storage: You do not need to store this medicine at home — it is stored and prepared at the clinic or hospital. If you are ever given a prepared solution to take to another facility, keep it refrigerated between 36°F and 46°F (2°C and 8°C) and do not freeze it. Keep it away from direct light and out of the reach of children.
what_to_avoid: Avoid any planned surgeries or dental procedures without first telling your doctor you are on this medicine, as it can slow wound healing. Avoid activities that put you at high risk of cuts or injuries. Do not get live vaccines (such as the nasal flu vaccine) while on this treatment without your doctor's approval. Avoid becoming pregnant — use reliable birth control during treatment and for at least 6 months after your last dose. Do not breastfeed while taking this medicine and for at least 6 months after your last dose.
when_to_call_doctor: Call your doctor or go to the emergency room right away if you experience any of the following: unusual or severe bleeding (such as coughing up blood, blood in your urine or stool, or heavy vaginal bleeding), severe high blood pressure or a sudden severe headache, signs of a stroke (sudden numbness, weakness on one side of the body, trouble speaking, or vision changes), chest pain or shortness of breath, signs of a blood clot in the leg (swelling, pain, or redness in one leg), severe stomach pain, vomiting, or constipation, a wound that is not healing, signs of an allergic reaction during the infusion (rash, flushing, chills, dizziness, or trouble breathing), any new or worsening symptoms that concern you.
when_it_works: You may not feel any different right away. This medicine works quietly in the background to slow tumor growth. Your doctor will use scans and lab tests over time to check if the treatment is working. It is important to stay on your treatment schedule and keep all follow-up appointments even if you feel well.
special_populations: Elderly patients (65 and older) may have a higher risk of certain side effects, including blood clots, high blood pressure, and serious bleeding, and should be monitored closely. This medicine should NOT be used during pregnancy because it can seriously harm an unborn baby. Women who could become pregnant must use effective birth control during treatment and for at least 6 months after the last dose. Breastfeeding is not recommended during treatment and for at least 6 months after the last dose. The safety and effectiveness in children have not been fully established. Patients with kidney or liver problems should speak with their doctor, as extra monitoring may be needed.
